title: GlusterFS Replica 3 Explained: What It Protects—and What It Doesn’t
summary: Replica-3 volumes improve availability by keeping three copies of data, but they are not backups. Learn how failure, quorum, healing, and split brain affect a GlusterFS volume.
author: Eliware
content:
# GlusterFS Replica 3 Explained: What It Protects—and What It Doesn’t

Replica 3 is one of the most useful GlusterFS volume layouts for a small cluster. It keeps a full copy of each file on three bricks, normally distributed across three storage nodes. If one node or brick becomes unavailable, the remaining replicas can continue serving the volume.

That is valuable protection against a storage-node failure. It is not a backup.

The distinction matters because replication and backup solve different problems. Replication helps keep a service available when infrastructure fails. Backup helps you recover data after deletion, corruption, ransomware, operator error, or a disaster that affects the whole storage system. A reliable GlusterFS design needs both.

## What replica 3 actually means

A replica-3 volume has three bricks in each replica set. For a simple three-node volume, a file written to the volume is stored on all three bricks:

```text
                 ┌── node 1 / brick 1
client ─ volume ─┼── node 2 / brick 2
                 └── node 3 / brick 3
```

The client sees one filesystem namespace. It does not need to browse the brick directories or decide which copy to use. GlusterFS coordinates the replica set and presents the data through the mounted volume.

The price is capacity. Three full copies require roughly three times the raw space of the logical dataset, before filesystem and GlusterFS overhead. Replica 3 is a reliability choice, not a capacity-efficiency choice.

## What happens when one node fails?

Suppose node 3 loses power while nodes 1 and 2 remain healthy. The volume can generally continue operating from the two available replicas. New writes are recorded on the available bricks, while the unavailable brick falls behind.

When node 3 returns, GlusterFS heals the changes that occurred while it was offline. The amount of work depends on how much data changed, how long the brick was unavailable, and the condition of the cluster. A node coming back online does not mean that healing is complete.

Inspect the volume and heal state after a failure test:

```sh
sudo gluster volume status testvol
sudo gluster volume heal testvol info
```

Run these checks from a trusted GlusterFS server or an administrative client. Continue monitoring until the pending heal state reaches the result your operational procedure expects.

## Why quorum matters

A replica set needs enough healthy members to make safe decisions about writes. In a three-way replica, two available bricks provide a majority. If the cluster cannot establish the required quorum, GlusterFS may refuse writes or make the volume read-only rather than risk divergent copies.

This behavior can be surprising when the priority is simply “keep accepting writes.” In distributed storage, accepting writes without a reliable majority can create conflicting histories that are harder to repair than a temporary write failure.

Do not change quorum-related options casually to make a degraded test appear healthy. First understand the failure mode, the client behavior, and the recovery path you need. Treat volume-option changes as operational changes that require verification.

## Replication is not a backup

If a user deletes `project-final.tar`, that deletion is normally replicated too. If an application corrupts a database export and writes the corrupted version successfully, the replicas can faithfully preserve the corrupted version. If an attacker reaches the mounted volume with write access, three copies do not provide three independent recovery points.

A backup should provide a separate recovery path, such as:

- a separate volume or storage system;
- snapshots with a documented retention and recovery process;
- an offline or otherwise isolated copy;
- a different administrative boundary; and
- regular restore tests.

A snapshot stored on the same failure domain may be useful for quick rollback, but it should not be your only backup. Decide what you need to recover from and how far back you need to go, then test that procedure before an incident.

## What is split brain?

Split brain occurs when GlusterFS cannot determine which copy of a file or directory entry is authoritative. This can happen when different replicas accept or record conflicting changes. The result is not simply “one copy is old.” There may be no safe automatic answer.

GlusterFS documentation describes several forms of split brain:

- data split brain, where file contents differ;
- metadata split brain, where attributes differ; and
- entry split brain, where directory entries, GFIDs, or file types differ.

Start diagnosis with the heal information command:

```sh
sudo gluster volume heal testvol info
```

Do not resolve a split-brain file by guessing which brick looks correct from the underlying filesystem. Brick paths are implementation details, and manually editing brick contents can make the situation worse. Use the documented GlusterFS healing and resolution procedures, preserve evidence, and record which copy was selected and why.

The [official split-brain troubleshooting guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/main/Troubleshooting/resolving-splitbrain/) explains the diagnostic output and available resolution methods.

## A safe failure exercise

Before trusting a new volume, perform a controlled test with disposable data:

1. Create a small test file on the mounted volume.
2. Confirm that all expected bricks are online.
3. Stop GlusterFS or power off one test node.
4. Read the existing file from the client.
5. Create a second test file while the node is unavailable.
6. Restore the node.
7. Check volume status and pending heals.
8. Confirm that both files are present after recovery.
9. Record the observed client errors, recovery time, and operational steps.

The test should match your real topology. A clean three-container demonstration does not prove that a production network partition, disk failure, node replacement, or Kubernetes rescheduling event will behave exactly the same way.

## Keep the failure domains real

Three replicas only provide three-node protection if the three bricks are actually separated. These layouts are not equivalent:

```text
Good:                         Misleading:
node 1 / disk 1              node 1 / disk 1
node 2 / disk 2              node 1 / disk 2
node 3 / disk 3              node 1 / disk 3
```

The second layout can lose all copies when one server, host, controller, or local storage subsystem fails. Keep each brick on its intended node-local persistent volume and understand which failures your infrastructure shares.

This is why the Eliware storage design keeps one Gluster brick on each of three nodes and persists both brick data and Gluster control-plane identity. Recreating a container should not silently create a new peer identity or erase the volume definitions that describe the cluster.

## Replica 3 versus an arbiter volume

An arbiter layout uses three replica members but stores full data on only two of them; the third stores metadata used to help make consistency decisions. It can reduce raw capacity use while retaining important split-brain protections, but it is not the same as three full data copies.

Choose between full replica 3, an arbiter design, or another volume type based on your capacity, availability, failure-domain, and workload requirements. Do not select a layout solely because its replica number sounds safer.

The official [GlusterFS architecture guide](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Quick-Start-Guide/Architecture/) describes replicated, distributed-replicated, and dispersed volume types.

## The operational checklist

For every replicated volume, know:

- where each brick is located;
- which failure domains the bricks share;
- how much raw capacity replication consumes;
- how to inspect peer, brick, and volume status;
- how to inspect and monitor pending heals;
- how to respond to split brain;
- what the client sees during a node failure;
- where independent backups are stored; and
- how to restore data without relying on the live replicas.

GlusterFS can make a shared filesystem remain available through a node failure, but it does not remove the need for storage operations. Availability, consistency, and recoverability are related goals—not interchangeable words.

## Where Eliware fits

The Eliware GlusterFS project uses a protected replica-3 `gluster` volume for shared console state and keeps application volumes separate. The operator console exposes volume status, healing, snapshots, quotas, audit records, and access controls, but it does not turn replicated storage into a backup system.

That boundary is intentional. The safest storage platform is one that makes its guarantees clear. Use replica 3 to improve availability, use independent backups for recovery, and test both before you need them.

If you are starting from scratch, begin with our [EL10 installation and first-volume guide](https://glusterfs.eliware.org/). For the underlying client and volume model, see the official [GlusterFS client setup documentation](https://docs.gluster.org/en/latest/Administrator-Guide/Setting-Up-Clients/).
